comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: The serial run received the identical prompt and the same explicit list of modules, functions, and required git patch workflow.

comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel decomposed by child-agent breadth; serial used one sequential owner. Both ownership plans still covered all requirement patches.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: The parallel parent had the full prompt and child-agent protocol evidence, then produced one integrated patch set rather than leaving incompatible component contracts unresolved.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: The serial main agent kept all context in one trajectory and produced sequential commits for the same files and requirement slugs.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel introduced child handoff boundaries, but no evidence shows a missing requirement, stale handoff, or unresolved interface contract; serial avoided those boundaries by design.

comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel had child result retrieval and join work, while serial had no child lifecycle; neither left a missing return, abandoned implementation, or trapped verifier result.

comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: The serial run produced ten requirement patches in one workspace through sequential commits, avoiding shared child writes entirely.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel had more shared-state exposure, but no concrete collision, overwrite, or artifact contamination materialized; serial was simpler but reached the same deliverable state.

outcome_analysis.explanation: The official outcome is not discordant: both completed evaluations have solution_passed true and both harness summaries report the task resolved. The concrete task-solving difference is that parallel used child-agent fan-out and parent integration, while serial used one sequential main-agent trajectory. That difference did not change delivered requirement coverage, patch collection, or final evaluator acceptance.
